title: Muse can only be started from a laptop; the phone can decide on a round but never ask for one
locations: src/web/mcp/AGENTS.md (Connect: "Hosted connectors need OAuth, not built")
evidence: /auth/tokens offers one way in: a `claude mcp add --transport http ... --header` command for Claude Code. /mcp takes only a static bearer token and the area doc says hosted connectors need OAuth, which is not built, so the Claude phone app cannot attach. Nothing in the PWA asks for a round or carries a question: the Today card ("Muse: 2 outfits, 2 pieces to consider") appears only after an agent on a laptop calls finish_round.
user_impact: The household user standing at the closet with a phone cannot ask Muse anything ("what do I wear to the wedding", "find me a rain boot"). Styling help happens only when someone sits at a laptop and runs a round, so for the other household member Muse effectively does not exist.
recommendation: Decide the 0.1 story explicitly. Either (a) implement OAuth for /mcp (authorization-server metadata under /.well-known, which today answers {}) so the Claude mobile app can attach as a custom connector, or (b) add an in-app "Ask Muse" request: a small synced `muse_request` row (free text plus optional garment or trip) written from Today, the wishlist or a trip, returned by get_suggestion_feedback as `requests`, and answered by the existing round card. (b) keeps the phone-first rule and needs no new auth surface. In both cases say on /auth/tokens which clients can connect.

votes.reason: The code backs the claim. src/web/mcp/AGENTS.md says "Hosted connectors need OAuth, not built". /.well-known/* answers {}. No "ask Muse" or muse_request exists in src. The tokens page only has the Claude Code flow. The phone cannot start a Muse round. Muse is an optional agent-driven feature and the phone can still decide on rounds, so this is a feature gap and not a defect. I would rate it P2 and not P1.

The mechanism holds. AGENTS.md line 15 says hosted connectors need OAuth and it isn't built, and the README describes Muse as started only by a connected agent. The severity is overstated, so I'm calling it refuted at P1. Muse is an optional agent add-on, not the app's core job. Cataloging, outfits, the calendar and sharing all work on the phone. The phone can already decide on a round and see its Today card and notifications. The agent runs on a laptop by design, and a household of 2 users doesn't need Muse reachable from the phone for the first tag. Nothing is lost or exposed, so it is a contained capability gap, not serious reliability risk. The fix is also large (an OAuth authorization server, or a new synced muse_request table with API, MCP and offline-queue parity). That is a post-0.1 feature, not a blocker. The cheap 0.1 part is the last line of the recommendation: state on /auth/tokens which clients can connect. Overall this is P2.

title: Saved outfits fills with unnamed planner and "Wear this" one-offs; deleting a planned entry orphans its outfit
evidence: Demo persona: the Saved tab opens with 10 unnamed "Winter parka, Plaid flannel, Black jeans, ..." tiles ("Planned Nov 20") ahead of the 26 named outfits. One "Wear this" on Today added outfit 39, and one "Plan my week" added 4 more. I removed four auto entries (Nov 15-17) with the calendar's ×; their planner-made outfits stayed in Saved with no label ("Winter parka, Gym tank, Grey sweatpants, Running shoes" and three others). removeEntry never calls removeUnheldOutfits, although Undo, Change and the re-plan do. The same list is the "pick a saved outfit" picker on Change outfit and on a trip's + Add, where 16 machine composites sat above "Office uniform".
user_impact: After two months of weekly planning, a user's curated outfits sit under about 60 unnamed machine ones in three pickers, and the list cannot be cleaned without deleting them one at a time.
recommendation: Give outfits an origin and make the lists respect it. `removeEntry` applies Undo's rule (drop a planner-created outfit that nothing holds). Saved defaults to outfits the person named, saved or adopted (adoptPlannerOutfit already models this), with planner and idea one-offs behind a "Worn and planned" segment. The calendar and trip pickers use the same default. This is one rule at the outfit model, not three list filters.

votes.reason: The code claim holds. removeEntry (src/web/calendar/entry-actions.ts) calls only deleteEntry plus selfie byte cleanup and never calls removeUnheldOutfits. The week-plan docs list Undo, the swap and Change as the callers of that rule, and calendar delete is not among them. A planner-made outfit therefore stays in Saved after its entry is removed. I did not reproduce the 10 unnamed tiles or the picker ordering. Severity: this is list clutter with no data loss or security impact, and the outfits can still be deleted one at a time, so I rate it P2 rather than P1.

The mechanism holds. removeEntry in src/web/calendar/entry-actions.ts only calls deleteEntry and never removeUnheldOutfits, while replace.ts and plan.ts do call it. Planner-made outfits therefore stay behind when an entry is deleted. The impact is clutter, not breakage. No data is lost, nothing is insecure, and no core job becomes impossible. Named outfits stay present and usable, only pushed down in Saved and in the two pickers. Outfits can be deleted one at a time, and in a two-user household the "about 60 unnamed" figure is a projection. I would rate it P2: contained and annoying, but not a serious or reliability risk. The fix direction (an outfit origin plus one rule at the model) is reasonable, but the cheap core, making removeEntry apply Undo's rule, is the real fix. The "Saved defaults to named outfits" filter is a separate UX choice that should not be bundled in.

title: Muse's direct writes (calendar, trip, wishlist, garment edits) carry no attribution in the app
evidence: As Muse I called schedule_outfit(outfit 9, Nov 21), plan_trip_outfit("Lisbon dinner", trip 2), add_garment_from_link(destination wishlist) and update_garment(notes on garment 74). user_impact: The owner finds plans, trip outfits and wishlist items they never made and cannot tell that an agent did it, when, or how to reverse it. That undermines trust in handing an agent a write token.
recommendation: ToolContext.tokenId is already the provenance key for suggestions; extend it to every MCP write. Either record `planned_by: 'agent'` plus the token on calendar entries, trip outfits and garments an agent creates and show the token's name as a badge where "Auto" shows today, or add one "Agent activity" list under Profile > Agent Access (last N writes per token, each linking to its object). votes.reason: Confirmed in part: the only MCP write trace is the log line ('by user N (MCP)'), and tokenId is used for suggestions only. plannedBy exists on entries but only user/auto. Contained trust/UX gap, not a defect that breaks a job.

title: A partner opening an invite signed out loses it at sign-in, and the invite copy is written for the wrong person
evidence: Signed out, the invite link shows "Invitation from Theo ... You need to log in or create an account" with Login and Register links. After signing in as fresh@ the browser lands on /auth/profile and the invitation is gone; the link has to be opened a second time. The invitee reads "They can view all your garments but cannot edit, add, or delete anything", which is the grantor's wording. After Accept the landing page is Profile#sharing, not Theo's wardrobe.
user_impact: The household partner's first contact with the app is a dead end. They register, see an empty profile, and have to go back to the message and tap the link again; the copy suggests they are giving access rather than receiving it.
recommendation: Carry a `returnTo` (through safeReturnTo) from the invite page's Login and Register links, through both posts, back to the invite. The same parameter lets sign-in land on Today instead of Profile. Write the invite page for the invitee ("You can view Theo's garments; you cannot change them"). After Accept, navigate to /wardrobe?ownerId=<grantor>.

votes.reason: Confirmed: both login (routes.tsx:135) and registration (208) redirect unconditionally to PROFILE_PATH with no returnTo, so the invite is dropped. Copy and post-accept landing claims are screenshot-based and plausible. A first-contact dead end, but recoverable by reopening the link.

title: Sharing covers the garment grid only: a partner cannot see outfits, the plan or laundry, and View-only still shows prices and private notes
evidence: As fresh@ with VIEW on Theo: the closet, capsules and wishlist are visible, including Muse's need and its budget. /wardrobe/44?ownerId=1 shows "Price $399.00" and the note "Promotion burst. user_impact: The household jobs that actually involve two people (one does the wash, "what are you wearing Saturday", packing together) cannot be done by the partner. Meanwhile a View-only partner sees what each piece cost and the owner's private notes, which spoils a gift or a quiet purchase.

Laundry is the cheapest and the most household-shaped: a MANAGE grantee gets the Laundry tab and "Mark washed" over ?ownerId=, since the domain function already takes it for MCP. votes.reason: Confirmed in code: the garment page renders price and notes unconditionally, with only wears, cost and repairs gated on isOwner. Outfits, calendar and laundry are owner-scoped by design. This is a scope decision plus a small privacy leak of price and notes to View grantees, so P2 fits.

title: Search matches one literal phrase in name, brand or notes: "blue shirt" and "blazer navy" find nothing
evidence: Demo closet (80 garments): "navy blazer" gives 1 result; "blazer navy" gives 0; "blue shirt" gives 0 (Blue oxford, Western denim shirt and Plaid flannel are all blue shirts); "jcrew" gives 0 where "J.Crew" gives 13. "tee" returns 15, including Navy blazer, Denim jacket and Olive chinos through their notes. MCP search_garments {keyword: "blue shirt"} is also 0, so Muse inherits it.
user_impact: The natural way to find a garment (colour plus kind) returns "0 results" and the user falls back to scrolling 80 tiles or using the filter sheet.
recommendation: Make the keyword a token AND-search over one searchable text per garment (name, brand, colour labels, type and category labels, notes last). Split on whitespace and require every token to match; rank name and type hits above notes. Fix it in the shared `searchFilters`/`containsPattern` path so the grid, the API and search_garments all benefit. No full-text index is needed at household size.

votes.reason: Confirmed: queries.ts applies one ilike of the whole trimmed keyword over name, notes and brand. There is no tokenizing and no colour or type label matching, so 'blue shirt' and 'blazer navy' miss. A core finding job degrades but filters remain, so P2.

title: Bulk edit sets one property per round and cannot add to a capsule, archive, wash or select all

title: Link import reports "Filled in from the page" when it only read a shop's title or home page
evidence: Five real shop links; some were seed URLs that may be stale. patagonia.com returned a 3.3 KB shell (log: "title extracted, 0 of 0 photos") and the form opened with Name = "Patagonia Outdoor Clothing & Gear", no category or brand, under the green notice "Filled in from the page. Check everything before saving." uniqlo.com gave Name "Mens Merino Sweater | UNIQLO US" with no brand and no price. A discontinued allbirds URL redirected to the home page and gave "The World's Most Comfortable Shoes". J.Crew and Reigning Champ (JSON-LD) imported well: name, brand, price, type and photos. Colour came back empty or "pattern" on all five, even with "heather-grey" in the URL. MCP suggest_garment returns the same notice to Muse.
user_impact: On shops that serve an app shell or a redirect, the user gets a form that claims success with a marketing headline as the garment name. They either save junk or retype everything, and Muse cannot tell a weak read from a good one.
recommendation: Give `extractProduct` a confidence value: `product` (JSON-LD, or OG with product tags), `page` (OG only) or `title-only`. For `title-only`, or a final URL that left the product path, show a warning notice ("Could not read the product; the link is kept") and prefill only the link. Strip a trailing "| Site" from titles, fall back to og:site_name or the registrable domain for the brand, and feed the URL slug or variant to guess.ts for colour. Return the confidence in the MCP and API answers.

votes.reason: Confirmed: prefill.ts shows FOUND_DETAILS ('Filled in from the page') whenever product.source is non-null, including source 'title', the weakest tier. Only a null source gets NOTHING_FOUND. The reported '| Site' strip evidence is partly contradicted, since titleFields already cuts after the last ' | ', but the og:title path would not be cut. The false-success notice holds.

title: The Type filter appears only after a category has been applied, so "shirts" takes two trips through the sheet

title: "Plan my week" lands on the current week, so most of what it planned is off screen; banner rows are not links
evidence: On Friday Nov 13 I pressed Plan my week while viewing /calendar?week=2026-11-15. The answer was /calendar (Nov 8-14) with a text banner "Planned 4 outfits for your week: Sunday, Nov 15 · All day: Rain shell, ..."; every planned day was on the next page. The banner lines have no thumbnails and are not links. Because "your week" is today plus six days, from midweek on most planned days are always on the following page.
user_impact: The user presses the headline button and sees a calendar that looks unchanged below a wall of garment names; they must page forward to see or change what was planned.
recommendation: Redirect to the week holding the batch's first planned day, anchored at `#day-<first>`, and make each banner row a link to its day with the outfit collage thumb. Better still, render the calendar's default window as today plus six days rather than Sunday-Saturday, so the plan and the view share one model of the week.

title: The offline trip banner says packing needs a connection while ticks queue; the counter and "Saved" do not follow queued ticks
evidence: Offline on /trips/2 the banner reads "Offline: this is the trip from your last visit. Packing and changes need a connection." I ticked two garments: each showed "Waiting to sync", a toast said "2 changes waiting to sync", and both replayed on reconnect (server truth 3 of 15). Meanwhile the header still read "1 of 15 packed" and the form's status line still read "Saved". Today offline says "Wearing an outfit needs a connection": "Wear this" is not queued, although the garment page's "Wore today" is.
user_impact: A user packing in a basement or on a plane is told packing will not work, so they do not try, although it does work. Those who do try see a count that disagrees with the ticks.
recommendation: Derive the offline notice from the page's `data-offline-queue` kinds rather than a static string per page ("Ticks are saved on this phone and sync later; adding outfits needs a connection"). Have the outbox module update the packed counter and clear the autosave status when it queues. Decide whether Today's "Worn?" on an existing planned entry joins the outbox: it is the same write as a wear and the main morning action.

title: Signing in lands on Profile, not Today
evidence: POST /auth/login answers 302 to /auth/profile (PROFILE_PATH). Every sign-in in this audit opened on Account, Wardrobe Sharing, Notifications and so on, with Today one dock tap away. A session that expired mid-task returns to Profile, not the page the user was on.
user_impact: The first screen after sign-in is settings rather than "what do I wear"; a re-login loses the user's place.
recommendation: Redirect to `safeReturnTo(returnTo) ?? '/'`, with `returnTo` set by `decideSessionAccess` when it bounces a navigation to /auth/login. The same mechanism fixes the invite flow. Keep Profile as the landing page after registration only if onboarding lives there (city, week template); otherwise send new users to Today's empty state, which already links to both.

title: Removing a planned outfit uses the browser's native confirm() dialog
evidence: Tapping × on a calendar entry raises a native dialog "Remove this scheduled outfit?"; hx-confirm appears at 11 sites under src/web. In an installed PWA this shows as an OS alert titled with the origin, beside the app's own daisyUI sheets and Undo toasts. Wears and week plans already use Undo instead.
user_impact: A system alert breaks the look in an app that is otherwise carefully styled, and a confirm on every × slows the tidy-the-week flow.
recommendation: Use one pattern for reversible deletes: act at once and offer Undo in the SavedToast, as wears and week plans do. Keep a styled dialog only for irreversible ones (delete garment, delete account). Route the 11 hx-confirm sites through one component so the choice is made once.

title: A trip and the home calendar do not know about each other: Plan my week dresses trip days at home
locations: src/web/trips/AGENTS.md ("a standalone list of outfits ... not a date range over the calendar")

The calendar week shows no trip marker, and the trip's garments are not held back from home plans for those days. The new trip form also takes a Destination, but the forecast needs a second "Find" step on the trip page.

Resolve the destination's place at trip creation (run the Find on save) so the forecast is there on first view.

title: Sign-in limit is household-wide if TRUSTED_PROXIES misses Caddy, and the repo's own doc says it does
evidence: src/web/security/AGENTS.md says "Production's value does not yet cover Caddy: a homelab config change", while HEALTH_LIMIT's comment says "TRUSTED_PROXIES covers Caddy". If the first is true, request.ip is Caddy's for everyone: SIGN_IN_LIMIT (5/min keyed on request.ip, shared by the login page, API sign-in and registration) is one budget for the household, so anyone who can reach the login page sends 5 bad logins a minute and nobody can sign in. Nothing at boot or in /health/ready detects it. Not verifiable from this repo (production topology is in the private homelab repo).
user_impact: A household member mistyping a password, or any client looping bad logins, locks every phone out of signing in; refusal logs name Caddy instead of the client.
recommendation: Verify production and remove the contradiction in the docs. Then make the misconfiguration detectable in code: when a request carries X-Forwarded-For from a peer outside TRUSTED_PROXIES, log one warning per boot and report it as a degraded (non-failing) check in /health/ready, so the deploy shows it instead of a lockout.

votes.reason:
The doc contradiction is real. src/web/security/AGENTS.md:5 says "Production's value does not yet cover Caddy". rate-limit.ts:255 says "TRUSTED_PROXIES covers Caddy". docs/operations.md:29 tells the operator to set TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy network's subnet. Nothing at boot or in /health/ready detects a miss. The boot only logs "Trusted proxies: ...", and operations.md:50 relies on a manual check of the rate-limit warning.

The finding's P1 premise, that production is misconfigured, is not shown by anything in the repo. The same AGENTS.md says the MCP gate sits inside 172.16.0.0/12 and its real client IP is already visible, which suggests Docker subnets are covered. The "does not yet" line is probably a stale note from the #380 doc move. I did not check the homelab repo.

If TRUSTED_PROXIES really misses Caddy, the household lockout would follow, but that is conditional on an unverified deployment state. What actually holds is a doc inconsistency plus a missing detection safeguard, which is P2 hardening.

The mechanism is real but the P1 rating is overstated. (1) The repo's own docs point away from the failure state. security/AGENTS.md:6 says the closet-mcp-gate sits inside TRUSTED_PROXIES (172.16.0.0/12), and `MCP_LIMIT` sees the real client IP through it. A /12 docker range almost certainly also covers Caddy, so the "does not yet cover Caddy" sentence on line 5 looks stale, not a live bug. The finding's "the repo's own doc says it does" contradicts line 6. (2) Detection already exists. The boot logs `Trusted proxies: ...` (app.ts:168), and docs/operations.md:50 gives a post-deploy check that the 429 `for <ip>` warning names the client, not Caddy. The real gap is a docs contradiction and no automated check. (3) The impact is narrow. Only new sign-ins are blocked, at 5 a minute. Existing httpOnly cookie sessions on installed PWAs keep working, and the limit clears within a minute. A 2-user homelab has no attacker looping bad logins unless the host is exposed. The fix is also heavier than the problem. The /health/ready degraded check needs new state, and an XFF header from an untrusted peer can come from legitimate direct access, so it risks false warnings. The better fix is to correct the stale doc line and confirm the production value once. Severity is P2 (doc and config hygiene, plausible but contained); at most P3 if production is confirmed correct.

title: MCP tokens are all-or-nothing: a hostile or prompt-injected agent can rewrite every garment, including MANAGE-shared wardrobes
evidence: Every `mcp` token registers every tool (registerTools takes the full `tools` list) and acts exactly as its user. add_garment_from_link and add_inspiration return a hostile product page's title and text to the model; an injected instruction can then call update_garment across get_wardrobe's ids (own wardrobe, and any wardrobe shared with MANAGE via ownerId), set_capsule_membership, schedule_outfit, mark_worn and mark_washed. Nothing deletes, but there is no read-only token, no own-wardrobe-only token and no undo.
user_impact: One bad product page read by the agent can overwrite names, notes and tags across the owner's closet and a partner's shared closet, with only log lines to reconstruct from.
recommendation: Add a scope to the token at mint (Agent Access form): read-only vs read-write, and optionally own wardrobe only. Enforce it in one place: registerTools filters on the existing `writes` flag, and wardrobeFor refuses a foreign ownerId for an own-only token. Default new tokens to read-only.

votes.reason: registerTools receives the full tool list for every mcp token and there is no scope field. The case holds, but it is a prompt-injection hardening gap on a self-hosted household app and not a hole, and nothing deletes. P3 fits better.

title: Public /mcp parses the body before authenticating, never counts refused calls, and counts a 100-call batch as one request
evidence: requireToken is a preValidation hook, so Fastify parses up to 1 MiB of JSON for an anonymous caller before the 401 (the API moved its token check to onRequest for exactly this reason, src/web/api/token-auth.ts). MCP_LIMIT is a preHandler after auth and "an unauthenticated call is a 401 there and never counted", so the internet-facing gate has no limiter at all for anonymous posts, each a JSON parse plus one token-hash statement. With a valid token, the SDK accepts a JSON-RPC batch of up to MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 100 messages per POST, so 120 requests/min is up to 12,000 tool calls/min, e.g. 100 concurrent get_garment_photo reads base64'd into one answer.
user_impact: Anyone who finds the public MCP host can load the database pool and event loop that the household's phones share; a runaway or hostile agent gets 100 times the documented budget.
recommendation: Move requireToken to onRequest. Add a per-address checker for refused credentials on /mcp (HEALTH_LIMIT's pattern). Count tool calls, not HTTP requests: either refuse array bodies before the SDK (the current MCP spec dropped batching) or charge MCP_LIMIT once per message in registerTools' wrapper.

votes.reason: requireToken is a preValidation hook, so the body is parsed before the 401. MCP_LIMIT is a route rateLimit after auth, and the handler passes request.body straight to the SDK transport, so one HTTP request can carry a batch. The public gate also has no limiter for anonymous or refused calls. The case holds. P2 fits.

title: Every garment and outfit has a permanent public share id that cannot be revoked or rotated
evidence: shareableId is a randomUUID set on insert for every garment, outfit and file, and no code path changes it (no rotate or stop-sharing function exists). /share?shareableId=...&type=... is public and has no opt-in: the id is live from creation. The Share menu item renders for `model.canEdit`, so a MANAGE grantee can copy the public link of each garment; removing their share (removeShare) leaves every link working, as does the owner regretting a link they sent.
user_impact: A link sent once, or collected by a former MANAGE grantee, shows the item's name and photo (an outfit: all its garments) to anyone for the life of the row; the only remedy is deleting the garment.
recommendation: Make public sharing a state of the row rather than a constant: mint the id on the first Share tap (nullable column, or a rotation), and add Stop sharing, which nulls or rotates it. /share and /file/watermark then 404 for it. Outfits and garments share the one helper.

votes.reason: shareableId is a notNull UUID set on insert for file, garment and outfit. The schema has no nullable or rotate path, so a link can't be revoked. P2 fits.

title: Invite links never expire, need no step-up, and a share survives the password change meant to end a compromise
evidence: POST /wardrobe-share/create-invite-link takes `permission: MANAGE` with a session alone (no checksPassword, no ACCOUNT_LIMIT). acceptInvite checks only that the token is unanswered; wardrobe_share has created_at but nothing reads it as an expiry. updatePasswordHash revokes sessions, both token kinds and push devices, not shares or open invites. So a borrowed unlocked phone or stolen cookie mints a MANAGE link, accepts it from another account, and keeps write access after the owner signs out and changes the password, which is the outcome the step-up rule exists to prevent for tokens. An open link pasted in a chat stays claimable by whoever finds it, indefinitely.
user_impact: Changing the password after a scare does not remove an attacker's edit access to the wardrobe; old invite links stay live until someone notices them in Profile.
recommendation: Treat granting MANAGE as handing out a credential: checksPassword plus ACCOUNT_LIMIT on creating a MANAGE invite (VIEW can stay one tap). Titled resources are copied inline at each use: "InsightGarment" 11 times, "WishlistGarmentRef" 7, "OutfitGarment" 6, "BrandSize" 5, "GarmentPhoto" 4. 297 enum sites are emitted as anyOf of single-value enums (GarmentPhoto.cutoutStatus is six one-value branches). The /changes item is an anyOf of 11 objects with no discriminator on `resource`. Expected effect, not run here: swift-openapi-generator or openapi-generator would emit one nested type per copy and a try-each-branch decoder for the feed.
user_impact: The first native client either hand-writes its models, making the spec decorative, or ships a mapping layer between identical generated types. The 31k-line file is also unreviewable in PRs.
recommendation: Fix it once in the emitter (scripts/api-spec.ts transform), with no wire change: hoist every titled schema into components.schemas by title and fail on one title with two shapes; collapse an anyOf of single-string enums into one `enum`; add `discriminator: { propertyName: 'resource' }` to the feed's change union. Assert in scripts/api-spec.spec.ts that no titled schema appears inline.

votes.reason: Confirmed in part: 'InsightGarment' title appears 11 times inline in openapi.json as claimed. Native codegen would produce duplicate types. Contained to future client work, no wire change needed. P2 fits, arguably P3 until a native client exists.

title: A native client cannot tell which optional features or which build a server has
evidence: With WEATHER_ENABLED=false, `weatherApiRoutes` is never registered. The committed spec still documents its 11 operations (getWeather, searchPlaces, setWeatherHome, getTripWeather and others) because api-spec.ts passes a stand-in. Those paths then answer a problem 404, the same as an unknown id. GET /me returns only { id, email, timeZone, today }. info.version is the constant `v1`, and I found no response field carrying the build.
user_impact: A client on a weather-off server shows broken weather screens or must probe and guess from 404s. An app newer than the server cannot explain why an operation is missing.
recommendation: Add `features: { weather, push }` and `version` (APP_VERSION) to the Me resource, or a public GET /api/v1/server, sourced from WebConfig. Say in the spec that weather operations exist only when `features.weather` is true.

title: The changes feed omits resources the API writes, and the week template's sync stamp is read by nothing
evidence: The plan (section 7) lists the week template as a synced root. The trigger stamps `user.week_template_revision` on every template write, but a grep of src finds no reader (only schema.ts and a comment in sync-tables.ts). Device A does PUT /week-template; device B's /changes carries nothing. Also absent from the feed: outfit rules (GET /style-profile returns `rules`, but a rule write does not move style_profile's revision), garment clashes, wishlist needs and the Muse inbox, weather settings, and looks (the last by owner decision). The feed doc mentions the rules and template gap in one clause; the wire contract does not state which resources are feed-backed.
user_impact: A native offline store shows a stale week template and stale outfit rules after an edit on another device, with no signal to refetch. The client author learns which screens are online-only by trial.
recommendation: Decide per resource and write it into listChanges' description as a table of feed-backed versus fetch-on-demand. Add the week template to the feed as a one-row-per-user entry using the revision the trigger already writes, and make outfit-rule writes touch style_profile (a SYNC_CHILDREN row plus a new migration). If the template stays out, drop the column and trigger. Keep clashes, the Muse inbox and weather settings online-only, but say so.

title: README quick start loses the 940 MB model on every update and names Postgres versions no tier tests
evidence: The quick-start compose mounts only `closet_data:/app/data`. MODELS_PATH defaults to /app/models, which is in the container layer, so `docker compose pull && up -d` recreates the container and downloads 940 MB from Hugging Face again; photos stay "Removing background…" until it finishes. Production avoids this with CLOSET_MODELS_DIR. The same section says "PostgreSQL 13+" and ships `postgres:17-alpine`, while nightly.yml and the root CLAUDE.md put every tier on 18. The memory need (about 5 GB per operations.md) appears only at README line 296.
user_impact: Anyone hosting from the README gets a slow, bandwidth-heavy outage of background removal after each update, on a database version nobody has proven.
recommendation: Add a `closet_models:/app/models` volume and a memory note to the quick start. State one supported Postgres floor that a tier actually runs: move the example to 18 with its /var/lib/postgresql volume, or add a 17 job to the nightly.

title: DATABASE_SSL=true never verifies the server certificate, and there is no connection-URL form
evidence: `ssl: config.ssl ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : undefined`, commented "pgvault's certificate is self-signed". Pointed at a managed Postgres over the internet, any on-path host can present its own certificate and read the password and all data. Config takes five DATABASE_* parts and no DATABASE_URL, which is what most managed hosts hand out. `DATABASE_SCHEMA` is actually the database name (README line 115 says so).
user_impact: A tailnet-only homelab is unaffected. Hosting on a VPS with managed Postgres silently runs unauthenticated TLS, and the operator has no setting to fix it.
recommendation: Give TLS a mode in loadConfig: `DATABASE_SSL=verify` (the default meaning of true) with an optional `DATABASE_SSL_CA` path, and an explicit `no-verify` that production's env sets for pgvault. Before the 0.1 tag freezes env names, add `DATABASE_NAME` and keep DATABASE_SCHEMA as a deprecated alias. Skip DATABASE_URL unless a host needs it.

votes.reason: Confirmed: src/db/client.ts sets ssl to { rejectUnauthorized: false } whenever config.ssl is true, with no CA or verify option. A real MITM exposure on untrusted networks. The homelab/tailnet deployment is unaffected, so P2 is right.

title: Background removal cannot be switched off and the image is amd64-only
evidence: main.ts always builds the ModelRunner and starts the 940 MB download at boot; serve() always starts the queue; the area doc says a leftover CUTOUT_MODE is ignored. The model child peaks at 2.9 to 3.3 GB RSS. On a 1 to 2 GB VPS the child is OOM-killed, each photo fails three attempts and ends on "Try again". The Dockerfile deletes onnxruntime's linux/arm64 binary and the image is published amd64 only, so a Raspberry Pi or ARM cloud host cannot run it.
user_impact: The cheapest hosts (ARM, small VPS) are excluded, or every upload shows a failed-cutout state. On the homelab, a broken Hugging Face URL gives the operator no clean way to run without cutouts.
recommendation: Add `CUTOUT_ENABLED` (default true) to config. When false, main.ts passes a runner that never becomes ready and skips the download, and uploads start through `initialCutoutState` as `none`, which already shows the original with the mask-editor pencil; no new state is needed. For ARM, delete the foreign-architecture binaries by TARGETARCH instead of always deleting arm64; publish multi-arch only when someone needs it.

votes.reason: Confirmed: the Dockerfile deletes onnxruntime linux/arm64 and says the image is amd64 only. config.ts has no CUTOUT_ENABLED, and the area doc says CUTOUT_MODE is ignored. Background removal is always on. It is a hosting-flexibility limit, not a defect for the actual deployment, so P2 is generous and P3 is arguable.

title: app.log is always written into the photo volume and never rotated
evidence: createLogger opens `join(config.DATA_PATH, 'app.log')` as a second synchronous sink beside stdout in every mode. A grep of src/logger.ts and src/maintenance finds no rotation, size cap or prune. Every request writes an access line. The file sits in the directory /file/** serves from (the files doc records it once leaked as /file/app.log) and is carried in every backup of the photo volume.
user_impact: On any host the data volume fills slowly until uploads fail and the boot's writability probe refuses to start. On hosts with read-only or ephemeral disks, the sink is the only reason logging needs a writable path.
recommendation: Make stdout the only default sink and the file opt-in (`LOG_FILE` path, unset by default). Docker and Loki already keep the container log in production. If the file stays, write it outside DATA_PATH and cap it in the nightly job.

votes.reason: Confirmed: logger.ts opens join(DATA_PATH,'app.log') as a second sink in both json and pretty modes with no rotation or cap in the code I read. It is slow growth inside the data volume, so a real operational hazard but contained. P2 fits.

title: Authentication-Results parser splits on ';' inside quoted strings, so attacker-controlled values can inject a passing method
evidence: `parseAuthenticationResults` does `withoutComments(header).split(';')` and then regex-matches `method=result` and `ptype.prop=value` per piece. RFC 8601 values can be quoted strings, and two fields in Fastmail's own topmost header are sender-chosen free text: `smtp.mailfrom` (the envelope local-part) and DKIM `header.i`. A message with From: owner@gmail.com (an allowed sender) and envelope sender `"x; dkim=pass header.d=gmail.com y"@evil.example` with valid SPF for evil.example would, if Fastmail echoes the quoted local-part, yield a piece ` dkim=pass header.d=gmail.com y"@evil.example`. METHOD matches `dkim=pass`, PROPERTY reads `header.d=gmail.com`, `passesFor` returns true, and the sender is trusted. The spec has no quoted-value case. Not verified against Fastmail's actual output (it depends on their MX accepting and echoing a quoted local-part), so treat as plausible.
user_impact: Someone who knows the order mailbox address and one allowed sender address could put arbitrary products in the owner's review list and make the server fetch up to 12 chosen public URLs per email. Nothing reaches the closet without a tap, and the fetcher is SSRF-safe.
recommendation: Tokenise the header properly (quoted strings and comments in one scanner) instead of split plus regex, and fail closed: refuse any header where a method name repeats with conflicting results or where a quoted string contains `;` or `=`. Preferably trust only `dmarc=pass header.from=<exact From domain>` or `dkim=pass header.d=`, whose values are DNS names and cannot carry quotes, and drop SPF-only acceptance. Add spec cases for quoted mailfrom and header.i injection.

The exploit is unverified. It needs Fastmail to echo a quoted sender-chosen smtp.mailfrom or header.i, and the attacker must know the order mailbox address and an allowed sender. Impact is bounded because nothing is imported without an owner tap and the fetcher is SSRF-safe. This is defense-in-depth hardening, so P3 fits better than P2.

title: The authorization-coverage guard does not require a matrix row for routes that take resource ids only in the body

user_impact: No user impact today. The guard that makes the matrix a guarantee has a hole exactly where an IDOR regression would land.

title: POST /push/test has no rate limit

recommendation: Add a per-user checker (a few per minute) and answer the existing 200 fragment with a "try again in a minute" state, as the link import's photo choice does.

recommendation: Have the nightly maintenance run delete cache rows that no `user_weather` home or here location and no trip destination references and that were last attempted more than about 30 days ago, with a row in its report.
